facts.text: Entropy, written S, measures how many microstates match a system's macrostate. A macrostate is the state you can measure, such as a gas's temperature, pressure and volume; a microstate is one exact arrangement of every particle and its energy that produces that macrostate. A macrostate that can be built in more ways has higher entropy: Boltzmann's formula is S = k ln W, where W is the number of microstates and k is Boltzmann's constant, and entropy is measured in joules per kelvin. A common mistake is to think entropy just means disorder or messiness; disorder is only a loose metaphor, and entropy really counts the ways particles and their energy can be arranged, which is why it is better pictured as energy spreading out than as mess. Entropy counts the ways energy can be spread out, and things drift toward the state with the most ways.

Two dice are a model of entropy: each exact pair of faces is like a microstate and the total is like a macrostate. Two dice can land in 36 ways; a total of 7 can be rolled 6 ways but a total of 2 only 1 way, double ones, so 7 comes up six times as often and is the most common total. This is the same counting of outcomes used in probability. Gas molecules are counted the same way: with four molecules in a box of two halves, the macrostate is how many molecules are on each side and a microstate says which molecule is where. There are 16 microstates; two on each side happens 6 ways, while all four on the left happens only 1 way, just 1 time in 16. Molecules constantly collide and trade energy, so a system keeps moving from microstate to microstate, roughly at random, and every microstate of an isolated system is taken to be equally likely, so the macrostate with the most microstates is the one most often found.

The second law of thermodynamics says the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases, and in any spontaneous process it increases. Everyday matter contains enormous numbers of particles, so spread-out macrostates have so many more microstates than bunched-up ones that a system is practically always found spread out. So a gas let into one half of an empty box spreads to fill the whole box, and hot coffee on a table cools as heat flows from it into the colder room air until both are at the same temperature; on its own, heat flows from hot to cold, never the reverse, and spread-out energy does not gather back up by itself. Nothing in the laws of motion forbids all the gas molecules gathering back in one half, but that state has so few microstates that it is never seen. For heat Q added gently at a steady temperature T, the entropy change is ΔS = Q/T, so the same heat raises entropy more at a lower temperature; that is why heat flowing from hot to cold raises total entropy: the colder object gains more entropy than the hotter one loses.

One part of a system can lose entropy if its surroundings gain more. When water freezes into ice in a freezer's ice tray, its molecules lock into an orderly crystal and the water's entropy falls, but the freezer uses electrical work to pump that heat out through its coils into the kitchen, and the room air gains more entropy than the water lost, so total entropy still rises. A freezer can move heat from cold to hot only with that supply of work: if it is unplugged, no heat is pumped out, heat flows from the warm room air back into the freezer until the inside reaches room temperature, and the ice warms and melts, its orderly crystal gone, as the energy spreads out again and total entropy rises. The second law also limits heat engines, such as car engines and power plants: no engine can turn heat completely into work, because some heat must be released to a colder place, and this limit on efficiency is the next topic in thermodynamics.

misconception: A common mistake is to think entropy just means disorder or messiness. Entropy counts the microstates, the ways particles and energy can be arranged, so it is better pictured as energy spreading out; water can even freeze into an orderly crystal, because the surroundings gain more entropy than the water loses.

lesson_markdown:
# Entropy: counting the ways

**If entropy means disorder, why does a neat crystal of ice ever form?**

Entropy measures how many ways the particles and energy in a system can be arranged. Things drift toward the state that can happen in the most ways, so energy spreads out. That one idea explains why hot coffee cools and why a gas fills its box.

## Start with two dice

Roll two dice. The exact pair of faces is like a **microstate**, and the total you call out is like a **macrostate**.

| Total | Ways to roll it (out of 36) |
|---|---|
| 2 (double ones) | 1 |
| 7 | 6 |

Seven comes up six times as often as double ones, because more pairs add up to it. It is the same counting of outcomes you use in probability.

## The same counting, with gas

1. **A macrostate hides many microstates.** The macrostate is what you can measure, such as how many molecules sit in each half of a box; a microstate says exactly which molecule is where.
2. **Entropy counts them.** Boltzmann's formula is S = k ln W, where W is the number of microstates, so more ways means higher entropy.
3. **Molecules keep shuffling.** They collide and trade energy, so the system hops from microstate to microstate, each one taken to be equally likely.
4. **The biggest count wins.** With four molecules in a two-half box there are 16 microstates: two on each side happens 6 ways, but all four on the left happens only 1 way.

Predict: what happens with the enormous number of molecules in a real box of gas? The spread-out states have so many more microstates that the gas is practically always found spread out. Nothing in the laws of motion forbids all of it crowding into one half; that state just has so few microstates that it is never seen.

## The second law

The **second law of thermodynamics** says the total entropy of an **isolated system** never decreases, and in any spontaneous process it increases. That is why hot coffee cools as heat flows into the colder room air until both are at the same temperature. By ΔS = Q/T, the same heat raises entropy more at a lower temperature, so the cold air gains more entropy than the coffee loses. (That formula is simplified: it holds for heat added gently at a steady temperature.)

## Not disorder

A common mistake is to think entropy just means disorder or messiness. Disorder is only a loose metaphor: entropy counts the ways particles and energy can be arranged, so picture it as energy spreading out.

Water freezing in a freezer really does form an orderly crystal, and the water's entropy falls. But the freezer uses electrical work to pump that heat out into the kitchen, where the room air gains more entropy than the water lost, so total entropy still rises. Unplug it, and heat flows back in until the ice melts.

The same law means no engine can turn heat completely into work, which is the next topic in thermodynamics.

## Check yourself

Nothing pushes a gas into the empty half of a box, so why does it end up spread through both halves?

Want to dig deeper? Ask a follow-up about heat engines or about what S = k ln W means.
